case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an ERISA plaintiff alleging imprudent investment management based on underperformance must plead a “meaningful benchmark” (i.e., a truly comparable alternative investment or set of comparators) to plausibly state a fiduciary-breach claim under Rule 8 as interpreted by Twombly/Iqbal.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), principally 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1) (fiduciary duties of prudence and loyalty) and the federal pleading standard under Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a) (as construed by Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly and Ashcroft v. Iqbal).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Ninth Circuit applied an unduly demanding pleading rule that effectively requires ERISA participants—before discovery—to identify a “meaningful benchmark” or near-identical comparator that matches the challenged fund in all salient respects (strategy, risk, fees, asset class, objectives). They contend this conflicts with ERISA’s focus on process (not outcomes alone) and with ordinary notice pleading: persistent underperformance, excessive fees relative to reasonably comparable alternatives, and allegations suggesting fiduciaries ignored readily available lower-cost or better-performing options should be enough to raise a plausible inference of imprudence. Petitioners and supporting amici emphasize that critical details about the fiduciary’s decision-making process and the plan’s internal monitoring are uniquely in defendants’ control, so requiring highly particularized comparator pleading functions as an ERISA-specific heightened pleading standard that screens out meritorious claims and undermines ERISA’s remedial purpose.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that underperformance allegations are only probative if measured against truly comparable investments, and that requiring a meaningful benchmark at the pleading stage is not a heightened standard but an application of plausibility: without comparators sharing key characteristics, courts cannot infer imprudence rather than differences in risk profile, investment style, time horizon, or market conditions. They contend that ERISA does not make fiduciaries guarantors of returns; investment outcomes vary even under prudent processes. A benchmark requirement prevents hindsight litigation and costly discovery fishing expeditions in high-stakes class actions, aligning with Rule 8’s gatekeeping function under Twombly/Iqbal. The United States, supporting respondents, similarly stresses that comparisons require shared characteristics and that plausibility depends on whether alleged comparators are sufficiently alike to make an inference of imprudence reasonable.
key_precedents: Va. Mil. Inst. v. United States, 508 U.S. 946 (1993) (noted for the Court’s general practice of awaiting final judgment before certiorari, discussed in the vehicle posture comparison to Parker-Hannifin)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007) (plausibility pleading framework underlying the comparator/benchmark debate)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009) (plausibility pleading framework underlying the comparator/benchmark debate)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas make the best point on the other side: when a complaint asks a court to infer imprudence primarily from underperformance, ERISA’s “like character and with like aims” language means comparability is often what makes the inference plausible rather than equally consistent with different risk or strategy. But I do not think that justifies embracing the Ninth Circuit’s “meaningful benchmark” framing as a governing requirement, because (as Justice Kagan warns) it is too likely to ossify into an ERISA-specific pleading screen inconsistent with Dudenhoeffer’s insistence on careful, context-sensitive scrutiny rather than checklists. The narrower, institutionally sound course is to vacate any categorical comparator prerequisite while making clear that Twombly/Iqbal already require dismissal where the alleged alternatives are plainly inapt or the complaint pleads no facts making “like aims” plausible. That addresses Justice Alito’s hindsight-and-discovery concern without foreclosing plausible process-based claims where salient monitoring facts sit with fiduciaries.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point is the institutional one: a court-announced “meaningful benchmark” requirement could harden into an ERISA-specific heightened pleading rule and, given fiduciaries’ control of monitoring records, screen out some meritorious process claims before discovery. But where plaintiffs elect to plead imprudence chiefly by comparative underperformance, § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s text—“enterprise of a like character and with like aims”—makes like-for-like comparability part of what renders the inference of imprudence probative at all, not a judge-made add-on; absent alleged similarities in strategy, risk, objectives, and fees, underperformance is equally consistent with lawful differences. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that we should avoid any rigid “near-identical twin” or checklist formulation, yet as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” supports applying ordinary Twombly/Iqbal plausibility to require enough comparator context to move the claim from speculation to a reasonable inference. Because that requirement flows from the statute’s own comparator language when the theory is results-based, Kagan’s procedural concern does not undermine the legal basis for dismissal on these pleadings.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor rightly caution that a rigid, label-driven “meaningful benchmark” rule could morph into an ERISA-specific heightened pleading barrier when monitoring-process facts are largely in fiduciaries’ hands, and Chief Justice Roberts sensibly urges a non-categorical approach. But where the complaint’s theory is results-based underperformance, § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s text—“like character and with like aims,” as Justice Barrett stresses—means comparability is not an extra hurdle; it is what makes the inference of imprudence plausible rather than equally consistent with different risk, strategy, or objectives under Twombly/Iqbal. Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” reinforces that courts should screen hindsight-driven claims before imposing discovery burdens, and requiring some pleaded salient similarities (not an identical twin) is simply ordinary plausibility applied to the plaintiffs’ chosen inferential theory. Plaintiffs can still proceed without detailed benchmarks if they plead concrete process red flags; they just cannot infer imprudence from performance alone without enough like-for-like context to make that inference reasonable.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Thomas’s textual reliance on §1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like character and like aims” language is the strongest Respondent point, and I agree it supports dismissing complaints that rest on plainly inapt comparators under ordinary Twombly/Iqbal plausibility. But I remain persuaded by Justice Kagan (and the Chief Justice’s narrower framing) that elevating “meaningful benchmark” into a quasi-prerequisite risks hardening into an ERISA-specific heightened pleading rule that Dudenhoeffer cautions against, especially where monitoring-process facts are disproportionately in fiduciaries’ control. The better approach is case-by-case, context-sensitive scrutiny: require enough context to make the underperformance inference plausible and reject obviously non-like alternatives, without demanding plaintiffs plead a fully specified like-for-like control fund before any discovery. That balance screens hindsight-driven suits while preserving ERISA’s remedial function for participants lacking internal monitoring records at the outset.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett make the Respondent side’s strongest point: when plaintiffs’ theory is comparative underperformance, §1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like character and like aims” language means some pleaded basis for similarity is often necessary to make returns probative rather than equally consistent with different risk or strategy. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that translating that into a “meaningful benchmark” pleading requirement risks hardening into an ERISA-specific gatekeeper contrary to Dudenhoeffer’s warning against special pleading screens masquerading as plausibility doctrine. Twombly/Iqbal already allows dismissal where comparators are plainly inapt; the better, textually coherent and workable middle ground is a holistic plausibility inquiry that demands enough context to make “like aims” plausible without demanding fine-grained like-for-like detail that is often uniquely within fiduciaries’ control pre-discovery (as Justice Sotomayor emphasizes). That approach addresses hindsight and discovery burdens while preserving viable process-based claims that plausibly allege sustained underperformance plus excessive fees and available reasonably comparable alternatives.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point—that Dudenhoeffer cautions against ERISA-specific pleading hurdles and that prudence is process-focused with many monitoring facts held by fiduciaries—deserves real weight. But when plaintiffs’ own theory asks the court to infer an imprudent process primarily from relative performance and fees, §1104(a)(1)(B)’s text (as Justice Barrett emphasizes) makes “like character” and “like aims” comparability part of what gives those outcome allegations probative force; without some pleaded basis of similarity, underperformance is just as consistent with different risk or strategy under Twombly/Iqbal. Chief Justice Roberts is right to resist a rigid checklist, yet rejecting any practical comparability requirement would, in operation, invite the hindsight-driven, discovery-frontloading suits Dudenhoeffer instructed courts to screen through “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny.” Properly framed, the Ninth Circuit’s benchmark talk should be understood as ordinary plausibility applied to a comparative, results-based claim—not as an ERISA-only heightened rule—and plaintiffs remain free to plead non-comparative “process red flags” without a tight benchmark.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that a rigid “meaningful benchmark” requirement could harden into an ERISA-specific heightened pleading screen and unfairly block process-based claims where monitoring facts sit with fiduciaries—counsels against adopting any categorical checklist. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, when plaintiffs choose a results-based underperformance theory, §1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like character and like aims” language makes some pleaded basis of comparability intrinsic to plausibly inferring imprudence rather than different risk/strategy, consistent with Twombly/Iqbal and Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny.” Chief Justice Roberts is right institutionally to avoid blessing the Ninth Circuit’s phrasing as a standalone rule, yet I do not see a way—without diluting ordinary plausibility review—to allow an outcome-comparison claim to proceed with no factual allegations that the proposed alternatives share relevant aims and characteristics. Therefore I remain with Respondent: no identical-twin demand, but context-dependent comparator allegations are required where the complaint’s engine is comparative underperformance.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s warning—that “meaningful benchmark” language can ossify into an ERISA-specific heightened pleading screen when process evidence sits with fiduciaries—has real force, and I agree with the Chief Justice that we should caution against any rigid, checklist-like comparator prerequisite. But where the complaint’s theory is inferentially results-based (underperformance), the text of § 1104(a)(1)(B) (“like character and with like aims”) makes some pleaded basis for like-for-like comparability intrinsic to whether the alleged facts are probative of imprudence at all, rather than equally consistent with different risk/strategy/time horizon; ordinary Twombly/Iqbal plausibility does that work without demanding an identical “twin.” Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” supports screening speculative, hindsight-driven comparative claims at the threshold, while leaving room for process-red-flag allegations to proceed without detailed benchmarks. Properly framed—as Justice Roberts urges—as non-categorical plausibility rather than a freestanding pleading element, the Ninth Circuit’s comparator talk can be understood as applying ordinary pleading principles to the plaintiff’s chosen underperformance premise.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas make the Respondent side’s best point: when a plaintiff’s theory is comparative underperformance, § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like character and with like aims” language means some pleaded basis for similarity can be necessary to make an inference of imprudence non-speculative. But I remain persuaded by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that translating that into an effectively mandatory, complaint-stage “meaningful benchmark” requirement risks hardening ordinary plausibility into an ERISA-specific gatekeeping rule that Dudenhoeffer warned against and that, as a practical matter, shifts too much informational burden onto participants where monitoring details are often in fiduciaries’ exclusive control. Twombly/Iqbal already empowers courts to dismiss where alleged comparators are plainly inapt (risk/strategy/objectives), without announcing a categorical prerequisite that could bar otherwise plausible allegations of sustained underperformance plus excessive fees. On my progressive pragmatic view, the administrable and fair line is context-sensitive plausibility review—screening bad comparators—rather than a rigid benchmark rule that would predictably chill meritorious process-based claims.

John Roberts.reasoning: Rule 8, as construed by Twombly and Iqbal, demands a context-specific plausibility inquiry, not an ERISA-specific categorical pleading rule that functions as a heightened standard. Consistent with Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer, 573 U.S. 409 (2014), courts should scrutinize ERISA imprudence complaints carefully to avoid hindsight claims, but plausibility can be shown through allegations of persistent underperformance and excessive fees relative to reasonably comparable alternatives without requiring near-identical “meaningful benchmark” pleading at the outset. Imposing a rigid benchmark requirement risks dismissing potentially meritorious claims where the most probative facts about monitoring and process are within fiduciaries’ control, contrary to ERISA’s prudence duty under 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1) and this Court’s preference for narrow, process-focused adjudication. A narrower holding vacating the Ninth Circuit’s categorical approach would preserve institutional legitimacy and leave room for dismissal where pleaded comparators are plainly inapt under ordinary plausibility principles.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence, 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), is textually process-focused, but Rule 8 as construed in Twombly and Iqbal still requires factual allegations that make an inference of imprudence plausible rather than merely possible. When a claim rests on “underperformance,” that inference depends on an apples-to-apples comparison; without alleging a meaningful benchmark sharing salient characteristics (e.g., strategy, risk, fees), the court cannot reasonably infer mismanagement rather than differences in investment profile. This is not an ERISA-specific heightened pleading rule but an application of ordinary plausibility pleading to the theory asserted, consistent with Dudenhoeffer’s instruction to apply Twombly/Iqbal in ERISA fiduciary-breach cases. Requiring a meaningful benchmark at the pleading stage prevents hindsight-based litigation and preserves the limited judicial role by filtering conclusory claims before burdensome discovery.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence under 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1) is not a guarantee of optimal returns, so a complaint alleging “underperformance” plausibly suggests imprudence only if that performance is measured against genuinely comparable investments; otherwise, the more obvious explanation may be different risk, strategy, or time horizon. Under Twombly and Iqbal, Rule 8 requires enough factual content to permit a reasonable inference of liability, and insisting on a “meaningful benchmark” is simply applying that plausibility screen rather than creating an ERISA-specific heightened pleading rule. As this Court explained in Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer, ERISA fiduciary-breach claims demand careful, context-sensitive scrutiny at the pleading stage to avoid costly, speculative litigation driven by hindsight. Requiring comparators with similar salient characteristics is a practical, administrable way to distinguish plausible imprudence claims from fishing expeditions that impose substantial discovery burdens on plans and sponsors.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence under 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1) focuses on the fiduciary’s process, and Rule 8 as construed in Twombly and Iqbal requires plausibility—not an ERISA-specific heightened pleading regime demanding near-identical comparators before discovery. Because the fiduciary’s monitoring and decisionmaking information is largely in defendants’ control, insisting on a “meaningful benchmark” as a rigid pleading prerequisite risks insulating imprudent practices from review and undermining ERISA’s remedial purpose for workers and retirees. Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer confirms that courts may police implausible theories at the pleading stage, but it does not justify converting process-based prudence claims into an outcomes-only comparator test that many participants cannot satisfy without access to internal records. Allegations of sustained underperformance and excessive fees relative to reasonably comparable options can plausibly support an inference of imprudence, with the adequacy of comparability to be tested on a fuller record.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rule 8, as construed by Twombly and Iqbal, demands plausible—not perfect—allegations; and ERISA’s duty of prudence under 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1) is primarily about a prudent process, not guaranteeing returns. Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer requires “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” of imprudence complaints and cautions against crafting ERISA-specific pleading hurdles, which a near-identical “meaningful benchmark” requirement risks becoming when key process facts sit with fiduciaries. A plaintiff alleging sustained underperformance and excessive fees can plead plausibility using reasonably comparable alternatives (not a match on every salient feature), leaving fine-grained comparability disputes for later stages. That approach preserves workability and statutory coherence without opening the door to hindsight liability.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Rule 8 as construed in Twombly and Iqbal requires enough factual matter to make an inference of liability plausible, not merely possible; when an ERISA prudence claim rests on underperformance, that plausibility ordinarily depends on allegations that compare the challenged investment to a sound, like-for-like benchmark rather than to inapt alternatives. ERISA’s duty of prudence, 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), asks what a prudent fiduciary “acting in a like capacity” would do in an “enterprise of a like character and with like aims,” and a complaint that offers no meaningful comparator typically supplies only a conclusory “a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently.” Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer instructs courts to apply “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the pleading stage to separate plausible claims from meritless ones, and requiring a meaningful benchmark in outcome-based underperformance allegations is an application of that ordinary plausibility inquiry rather than an ERISA-specific heightened pleading rule.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence under 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B) focuses on process, but when a complaint rests on alleged underperformance, plausibility under Rule 8 as construed by Twombly and Iqbal depends on whether the alleged comparisons actually support an inference of imprudence rather than differences in risk, strategy, or objectives. Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer instructs courts to conduct “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the pleading stage and to screen out allegations that do not plausibly suggest a breach, thereby limiting hindsight litigation and costly discovery. Requiring a “meaningful benchmark” (i.e., sufficiently similar comparators) is best understood as an application of that context-sensitive plausibility inquiry, not an ERISA-specific heightened pleading rule, because without comparability underperformance allegations are not probative of an imprudent fiduciary process. As a practical matter and to preserve administrable pleading lines, plaintiffs should plead comparators similar in salient respects so the court can reasonably infer imprudence from results-based allegations.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: ERISA’s prudence duty asks whether a fiduciary acted as “a prudent man … acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters” would act “in the conduct of an enterprise of a like character and with like aims,” 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), which textually makes “like” comparability central when a claim rests on relative performance. Under Twombly and Iqbal, a complaint must plead enough nonconclusory facts to make an inference of imprudence plausible, and without a meaningful benchmark or sufficiently comparable alternatives, underperformance allegations are equally consistent with different risk profiles, strategies, or objectives rather than a defective process. Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer applies this plausibility framework to ERISA prudence claims and instructs courts to apply “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the pleading stage to separate plausible claims from meritless ones; requiring a comparator that is meaningfully alike is a way of giving content to plausibility rather than imposing an ERISA-specific heightened pleading rule. Plaintiffs need not identify a near-identical twin, but they must plead enough about comparability to make the asserted inference of imprudence reasonable on the face of the complaint.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence under 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1) centers on the fiduciary’s decisionmaking process, and Rule 8 as construed in Twombly and Iqbal requires plausible—not near-conclusive—allegations before discovery. A categorical pleading requirement that a plaintiff identify a “meaningful benchmark” risks functioning as an ERISA-specific heightened pleading rule that can foreclose claims where key facts about monitoring and decisionmaking are uniquely in the fiduciaries’ control, undermining ERISA’s remedial purpose and procedural fairness. Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer instructs courts to apply “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” rather than bright-line pleading rules in ERISA imprudence cases, and comparator allegations should be one potential way—rather than a mandatory prerequisite—to make underperformance-based imprudence plausible. Plaintiffs must still plead enough facts to make imprudence a reasonable inference, but Rule 8 does not demand a truly identical alternative investment at the complaint stage.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether ERISA plaintiffs alleging an imprudent-investment claim based on underperformance must plead a “meaningful benchmark” (i.e., a truly comparable alternative investment) to plausibly infer fiduciary imprudence at the motion-to-dismiss stage.
case_analysis.legal_provision: ERISA fiduciary-duty provisions—principally 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B) (duty of prudence) (and related enforcement/remedial provisions in 29 U.S.C. § 1132).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Ninth Circuit applied an overly demanding pleading rule that effectively requires ERISA plaintiffs to identify, with detailed specificity at the complaint stage, a highly comparable benchmark or substitute investment to survive dismissal. They contend that this heightened requirement is inconsistent with ordinary Rule 8 pleading principles and ERISA’s context because plan participants typically lack access to the fiduciaries’ decisionmaking record before discovery. In their view, allegations of persistent underperformance, excessive costs, and readily inferable comparisons (including comparisons to available lower-cost or better-performing alternatives) should be sufficient to raise a reasonable inference of imprudence, with the finer details of comparability and fiduciary process to be tested on a fuller record rather than on the pleadings.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that underperformance allegations are inherently comparative, so a complaint must plead a meaningful benchmark—comparators sharing key characteristics (e.g., investment objectives, strategy, risk profile, asset allocation, management style, and fees)—to make an inference of imprudence plausible rather than speculative. They maintain that without a well-pled comparable alternative, courts cannot distinguish true fiduciary imprudence from permissible differences in investment strategy or risk/return tradeoffs, and that allowing bare underperformance claims to proceed would invite costly discovery and litigation pressure in cases that amount to hindsight second-guessing. The United States as amicus supporting respondents similarly emphasizes that the validity of inferences from performance comparisons depends on whether the comparator is genuinely comparable along material dimensions.
key_precedents: Va. Mil. Inst. v. United States, 508 U.S. 946 (1993)
Parker-Hannifin Corp. v. Johnson, 122 F.4th 207 (6th Cir.) (case presenting the same question)
28 U.S.C. § 1254 (certiorari jurisdiction referenced for interlocutory review context)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry concern is the strongest argument for Petitioner, but under Twombly/Iqbal we cannot allow discovery to supply the very predicate that makes an underperformance-only theory coherent; otherwise any market lag becomes a hindsight lawsuit. As Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, this is not an ERISA-specific heightened pleading rule barred by Hughes, but an application of ordinary plausibility to a comparative theory embedded in § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like capacity” standard—requiring some pleaded basis that the proposed alternative is similar in material respects (risk/strategy/fees). Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” reinforces that gatekeeping role at the pleading stage to avoid meritless, settlement-driven litigation, while leaving room for non-performance, process-based imprudence allegations that do not turn principally on relative returns. On a minimalist approach, the holding should be narrow: a meaningful benchmark is required only where the complaint’s breach theory depends principally on relative underperformance, not across all ERISA prudence claims.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s information-asymmetry concern is real, but it cannot rewrite Rule 8 or ERISA’s text: § 1104(a)(1)(B) asks what a prudent person “acting in a like capacity” would do, which necessarily turns on materially similar alternatives when the theory is underperformance. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, without some pleaded basis that the comparator matches on objective/risk/strategy/fees, “it did worse” is equally consistent with lawful risk-return tradeoffs as with imprudence, making the inference speculative under Twombly/Iqbal and inviting hindsight litigation. Dudenhoeffer’s insistence on “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the pleading stage supports, rather than undermines, requiring the minimal factual predicate that makes a performance-comparison claim coherent; Hughes’s caution against rigid categorical rules is satisfied by limiting this requirement to underperformance-based theories and not all prudence claims. Nothing in ERISA or the Federal Rules authorizes letting conclusory underperformance allegations proceed to discovery to search for a benchmark post hoc.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press a serious information-asymmetry concern, but Rule 8 as construed in Twombly/Iqbal still requires enough factual content to make imprudence a plausible inference rather than a hindsight label for market lag. Where the theory is underperformance, § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like capacity” prudence standard is inherently comparative; absent some pleaded basis that the proposed alternative is similar on material dimensions (risk/strategy/fees), the court cannot perform Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” without collapsing into speculation. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that is not a categorical ERISA-specific heightened pleading rule barred by Hughes, but an application of ordinary plausibility to a claim whose logic depends on a meaningful benchmark. Plaintiffs remain free to plead process- or fee-based indicia of imprudence, but an underperformance-only complaint cannot use discovery to search for a comparator that the pleading itself does not plausibly identify.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts is right that an underperformance theory is comparative and that Dudenhoeffer calls for “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the pleading stage, but I do not read Dudenhoeffer (or Twombly/Iqbal) to authorize a quasi-merits demand that plaintiffs plead a fully specified “meaningful benchmark” before any discovery. Justice Kagan’s framing—that this is merely ordinary plausibility review—risks, in practice, becoming an ERISA-specific heightened pleading screen because comparability details (risk controls, strategy constraints, institutional share-class availability, and fiduciary deliberations) are often uniquely in the defendants’ possession, a point Justice Jackson underscores. Hughes counsels against rigid shortcuts, and I worry a comparator-identification requirement for “underperformance-only” claims will predictably be applied rigidly, insulating imprudence where persistent lag plus excessive fees plausibly suggests a deficient process. Comparability can still be tested through Rule 12’s common-sense assessment and then on a record, without front-loading a benchmark showing that effectively denies participants access to justice in cases with real retirement-security consequences.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry point is serious, but it cannot erase Rule 8’s requirement that the complaint supply enough factual content to make the inference of imprudence plausible rather than merely possible; for an underperformance-based theory, that plausibility turns on whether the proffered comparison is materially like-for-like. As the Chief Justice notes, without some pleaded basis for comparability (risk/strategy/fees), a return gap is equally consistent with permissible risk–return tradeoffs as with imprudence, and Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” is meant to prevent hindsight-driven litigation at the pleading stage, not defer all context to discovery. Hughes affects my analysis only to the extent it warns against rigid, categorical shortcuts; properly framed, requiring a “meaningful benchmark” here is just ordinary Twombly/Iqbal applied to a comparative theory, and our holding can be limited to underperformance-only claims while leaving room for process- or fee-mismatch allegations that don’t depend on performance comparisons. Justice Jackson is right that plaintiffs need not negate every alternative explanation, but they must still plead a minimally informative comparator to anchor the inference of breach under § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s context-specific prudence standard.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor (and Justice Jackson) rightly emphasize information asymmetry, but that policy concern cannot rewrite Rule 8 as construed in Twombly/Iqbal by allowing a complaint to proceed on “it did worse” and then use discovery to search for a viable comparator. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, when the theory is underperformance-only, § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like capacity” standard makes comparability a necessary factual predicate; without some pleaded basis that the benchmark is similar in material respects (objective, risk/strategy, fees), a return differential is equally consistent with permissible risk/return tradeoffs as with imprudence. Dudenhoeffer’s instruction for “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” supports this gatekeeping at the pleading stage to avoid hindsight-driven litigation and settlement pressure, and Hughes’s warning against rigid categorical rules is satisfied by limiting any “meaningful benchmark” requirement to comparative-performance theories rather than all prudence claims. Separation-of-powers principles further counsel against creating an ERISA-specific relaxed pleading regime simply to improve access to discovery.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson rightly stress information asymmetry, but under Twombly/Iqbal the complaint must still supply enough nonconclusory facts to make imprudence a plausible—not merely possible—inference, and for an underperformance-only theory that plausibility turns on whether the proposed alternative is materially comparable. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, without some pleaded anchor on shared risk/objective/strategy/fee dimensions, courts cannot apply Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” without sliding into hindsight review and discovery-driven settlement pressure. Hughes does not require us to accept apples-to-oranges comparisons; consistent with Justice Kagan’s framing, “meaningful benchmark” is best understood as ordinary plausibility tailored to a comparative theory, while leaving room for other prudence theories (fees/process indicia) that don’t depend on performance comparisons. I therefore remain with Respondent on the narrow ground that a comparator is required when the claim’s theory rises or falls on relative performance.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry concern is the strongest point for Petitioner, but it cannot displace Rule 8’s requirement—under Twombly/Iqbal—that the pleaded facts make breach a plausible inference rather than a discovery-enabled fishing expedition. Where the theory is underperformance alone, the inference of imprudence depends on whether the proffered alternative is materially comparable (risk/strategy/objectives/fees); absent that anchor, the complaint is equally consistent with lawful risk–return tradeoffs and becomes impermissible hindsight review. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan rightly frame a “meaningful benchmark” not as a categorical safe harbor forbidden by Hughes, but as ordinary plausibility applied to a comparative theory that tracks § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like capacity” standard and Dudenhoeffer’s call for careful, context-sensitive scrutiny at the pleading stage. Participants remain able to plead other imprudence theories (e.g., concrete fee mismatches or self-dealing indicia) without the same comparator showing, so the requirement is narrow and textually grounded rather than a heightened pleading regime.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s point that an underperformance theory is comparative and that Dudenhoeffer requires “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny,” but I do not think that translates into a pleading-stage obligation to identify a “meaningful benchmark” with material-similarity detail that is often inaccessible absent discovery. Justice Kagan’s view that this is simply Twombly/Iqbal “ordinary plausibility” applied to a comparative theory still risks, in practice, converting plausibility review into a merits screen that privileges fiduciaries’ informational control and forces plaintiffs to negate risk/strategy explanations before they can learn what the fiduciary actually did. Hughes’s warning against rigid shortcuts cuts against ossifying comparator-identification into a quasi-element for performance-based claims; courts can instead ask whether the complaint alleges nonconclusory facts (duration/magnitude of lag, fees, readily available lower-cost options) that plausibly suggest imprudence, leaving finer comparability disputes for a record. Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s hindsight concerns are real, but they can be addressed by context-sensitive plausibility without imposing a de facto heightened pleading regime that predictably bars potentially meritorious ERISA claims at the courthouse door.

John Roberts.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence, 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), is judged against what a “prudent person acting in a like capacity” would do, and when a claim is premised on underperformance, plausibility necessarily turns on whether the alleged comparison is to a truly comparable alternative. Under Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer, courts must apply “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the Rule 12 stage to separate plausible imprudence claims from hindsight second-guessing, and requiring a meaningful benchmark is a narrow, administrable application of Twombly/Iqbal in this setting. This approach respects institutional interests in filtering meritless cases before costly discovery while still leaving room for plaintiffs who can plead a sound basis for comparison.
